analysis.one_liner: Bans hiring anyone under 18 to handle tobacco plants or leaves on farms.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health and labor committee in June 2023 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal labor law to make it illegal for farms to employ anyone under 18 in work that brings them into direct contact with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves. Current law treats farm work more leniently than other work when it comes to child labor, so 16- and 17-year-olds can legally work handling tobacco today. The bill would close that loophole for tobacco specifically, classifying such work as oppressive child labor, which is already banned.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 18 who work in tobacco fields, most of whom come from low-income and immigrant farmworker families. Tobacco plants contain nicotine that is absorbed through the skin, and child workers commonly suffer nicotine poisoning (nausea, vomiting, dizziness), along with exposure to pesticides and long hours in heat. Making this work illegal for minors would remove them from that exposure.

how_it_helps.text: Deems any employment of a worker under 18 with direct contact with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves as 'oppressive child labor' under the Fair Labor Standards Act, which is prohibited for all employers. [S2]

Removes tobacco-related agriculture from the existing carve-out that exempts agriculture from child labor protections beyond the standard rules, closing the gap that currently allows minors to legally handle tobacco. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco farms lose access to teenage workers, a labor source they have historically drawn on, and would need to hire adults instead. Child workers from families that rely on their earnings would lose that income.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco growers and working farm families

drawbacks.text: Some farmworker families rely on their teenage children's earnings from tobacco work; an outright ban removes that income with no replacement benefit for the family. [S2]

The bill targets tobacco but leaves minors of the same ages free to do hazardous work in other agricultural sectors, such as handling certain machinery or other crops, so the protection is narrower than a general upgrade of farm child labor rules. [S2]
Child labor rules in agriculture are historically weakly enforced, and even a prohibition on tobacco contact would depend on inspection and penalties actually being applied in the field. [S1]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: nicotine absorption through the skin makes tobacco handling unlike most farm work, and the bill targets exactly that contact rather than all youth farm labor. The real costs fall on a small number of low-income families who lose a source of teen earnings, and enforcement would determine whether the ban works in practice. It is a narrow fix, not a comprehensive solution to hazardous child labor in agriculture.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to its Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on June 12, 2023, joined by Sens. Brown and Blumenthal as cosponsors. [S3]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. [S4]
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco growers keep access to teenage workers, since nothing changed. Children under 18 remain legally able to work handling tobacco, with the nicotine exposure that comes with it.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban employment of children under 18 in tobacco agriculture.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — in the year and a half before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past committee referral. [S3]

industries.note: The bill would bar them from employing workers under 18 to handle tobacco, cutting off a labor source they use today. Their interest in keeping teenage field labor runs against the children's protection from nicotine exposure.

They do not employ the field workers directly, but child labor in their supply chain has drawn public scrutiny and litigation; a ban would raise leaf costs while cleaning up the supply chain they sell from.
